analysis.problem_summary: Determine whether a singly-linked list contains a cycle, returning true if any node can be reached repeatedly by following next pointers, and false otherwise.
analysis.intuition: If two runners race on a circular track at different speeds, the faster runner will eventually lap the slower runner and meet them again. We can apply this principle to a linked list using two pointers: a `slow` pointer moving one node per step and a `fast` pointer moving two nodes per step. If the list has no cycle, `fast` will safely hit the end (`null`). If a cycle exists, both pointers will eventually enter the loop, where `fast` closes the gap by one node in every iteration until both pointers meet at the exact same node.
approach: Initialize two pointers, `slow` and `fast`, both starting at `head`.
Enter a `while` loop that continues as long as `fast` and `fast.next` are not `null`.
Check if `slow == fast`. If they point to the exact same node reference, a cycle exists, so return `true`.
If the loop exits because `fast` or `fast.next` reached `null`, return `false` as the list is acyclic.
analysis.why_it_works: When there is a cycle of length $K$, both pointers will eventually enter it. Once inside, the distance between `fast` and `slow` along the cycle decreases by 1 in every iteration because `fast` gains 1 step on `slow` per step ($2 - 1 = 1$). Because the relative distance shrinks by 1 each step modulo $K$, the pointers are guaranteed to meet within at most $K$ iterations, accurately detecting the cycle without an infinite loop.
analysis.key_takeaway: Using fast and slow pointers moving at different speeds allows detecting cycles in linked structures in $O(n)$ time while maintaining $O(1)$ constant auxiliary memory.
analysis.time_explanation: If the list has no cycle, `fast` reaches the end in $N/2$ steps; if it has a cycle, `fast` catches up to `slow` in at most $N$ iterations, running in linear time total.
analysis.space_explanation: The algorithm only uses two pointer variables (`slow` and `fast`), requiring constant auxiliary space regardless of list size.

analysis.problem_summary: Determine if a linked list contains a cycle by checking for repeated node object references.
analysis.intuition: If we keep track of every node object we encounter during traversal, reaching a node that has already been stored indicates a cycle.
approach: Create an empty `HashSet` to store node memory references (`ListNode`).
Traverse the linked list starting from `head` using a pointer `curr`.
At each node, check if `curr` is already present in the `HashSet`.
If present, return `true` as a cycle is detected.
Otherwise, add `curr` to the set and move `curr` to `curr.next`.
analysis.why_it_works: Node references in Java are unique memory addresses. If a cycle exists, traversing the list will eventually hit a node that was previously added to the set.
analysis.key_takeaway: Using a hash set to record node identity provides an intuitive way to detect cycles at the cost of linear memory space.
analysis.time_explanation: We visit each node at most once. Hash set membership check and insertion operate in average O(1) time, yielding O(n) total time complexity.
analysis.space_explanation: In the worst case (or when a cycle exists), the hash set stores references for up to N unique nodes, requiring O(n) extra space.
